newsitem.title: MEXICO: Britain's Clarke seeks more investment in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Clarke seeks more investment in Mexico.

text.p: Britain is no longer willing to cede Latin American investment opportunities to the United States and is actively promoting greater trade with Mexico, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clark said on Wednesday.

Arriving in Mexico on New Year's Day for a seven-day official visit, Clarke told a news conference this would be his last foreign trip before British elections, which are likely to be called in the first half of this year.

"I've singled out Mexico as a country of particular interest," Clarke said upon arriving at the airport. "It seems to be taking off again. It could be one of the big success stories in the global economy."
Bilateral trade between Britain and Mexico is about $1 billion per year, and Britain is the second-largest investor in Mexico with a $4 billion portfolio, according to the British embassy.
But trade with Britain accounts for only 0.7 percent of all Mexican trade, the embassy said.

"Historically the British had strong connections in Latin America, but in modern times we have made the mistake of regarding this as a kind of United States-dominated part of the world," Clarke said. "That is a mistake."

Clarke is travelling with a contingent of potential investors, mostly from the banking and finance sector, to assess the investment climate in the wake of Mexico's economic crisis that began with the December 1994 peso devaluation.
"I'm impressed by the way Mexico is tackling the consequences of the effects of the crisis," Clarke said. "So far it is succeeding."

Also in the official delegation is Harry Bush, Britain's privatisations chief, who will preach the benefits of selling off state enterprises. Mexico is in the process of privatising railroads, airports and natural gas distribution but recently scaled back a plan to sell off a petrochemical unit.
Clarke also said guerrilla violence and a kidnapping epidemic are unlikely to scare off investors.
"It has not shaken international investor confidence in Mexico," he said.
